subject: physics

moments.title: Young's double slit
moments.body:
Newton had argued light was made of 'corpuscles'. Young presents a paper to the Royal Society showing that light passing through two narrow slits produces interference fringes — exactly what waves do, and what particles can't.

The paper is poorly received in Britain. Newton's authority is too great. The wave theory gains ground only after Fresnel develops it mathematically in the 1810s, and Foucault measures light speed in water (slower than in air, as waves should be — particles should be faster) in 1850.

quote.text: The supposition of waves... will explain a variety of phenomena which cannot easily be accounted for in any other way.

moments.takeaway: Light is waves. Newton was wrong. The wave model dominates for the next century.

moments.title: Taylor's faint-light interference
moments.body:
Taylor (a 23-year-old undergraduate) does an experiment to test whether interference is built up by individual photons. He photographs a diffraction pattern using light SO FAINT that on average only one photon is in the apparatus at a time.

Exposures take months. The interference pattern still forms. Each photon, individually, behaves wave-like.
moments.takeaway: Single particles interfere with themselves. Light is both wave and particle — and so are particles.

moments.title: Davisson and Germer — electrons diffract
moments.who: Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer, Bell Labs
moments.body:
Davisson and Germer accidentally heat a nickel crystal during an electron-scattering experiment, creating a clean single-crystal surface. They get sharp diffraction peaks in the scattered electrons.

The electrons interfere as waves with wavelengths matching de Broglie's prediction (lambda = h/p, 1924). Matter has wave properties.
moments.takeaway: Particles diffract. The wave-particle duality is not a property of light alone.

moments.title: Tonomura's single-electron build-up
moments.body:
Tonomura's team builds an electron biprism — an electrostatic analogue of Young's slits — and fires single electrons one at a time at a detector screen. They record where each electron lands.

In early frames there's a scatter of dots, looking entirely random. After tens of thousands of electrons, the dots accumulate into a sharp interference fringe pattern. Each electron — alone in the apparatus, no other electrons to interfere with — contributes to a coherent fringe pattern.
moments.takeaway: The interference pattern is genuinely the behaviour of a single particle, NOT the result of many particles colliding.

moments.title: Molecules of 2000 atoms interfere
moments.body:
The Vienna group sends giant molecules (functionalised oligoporphyrins, ~25,000 amu, ~2000 atoms) through a Talbot-Lau interferometer. Interference fringes form.

This pushes the wave-particle duality up by orders of magnitude in mass. Where the line is between 'quantum object' and 'classical object' remains unclear — and the existing answer is 'we haven't found it yet'.
moments.takeaway: Quantum interference works for molecules of biological scale. There is no obvious upper limit to wave-particle duality.

now.title: Wave-particle duality today
now.body:
Quantum mechanics' formalism (wavefunctions in Hilbert space) makes wave-particle duality natural — particles and waves are not separate things but different aspects of one quantum state. Decoherence theory explains why everyday objects don't show interference: the environment 'measures' them constantly, collapsing superpositions.

Applications: electron microscopy (sub-Angstrom resolution), neutron diffraction (probing magnetism), matter-wave interferometry (precision sensors, atomic clocks).
now.open_questions: What sets the boundary between quantum and classical? Is decoherence sufficient, or is something else needed (objective collapse theories)? Can macroscopic objects (viruses, bacteria) be put into superposition states?

reflection: Young's 1801 result was correct, but contradicted Newton's authority and was suppressed in England for decades. Foreign chemists (Fresnel, Foucault) had to demonstrate it before British physics accepted it. How do scientific authority and national pride bias the acceptance of well-supported results?
